problem_data.story:
The Gravity of Deception
by Alan E. Nourse (Adapted)

The chamber was cold and sterile, illuminated by harsh fluorescent lights that buzzed incessantly overhead. Miguel Ortiz followed the towering Crystalline guard down the polished corridor of the detention facility, his breath forming small clouds in the frigid air. He pulled his Earth-standard thermal jacket closer, shivering as his eyes took in the transparent holding cells lining both sides of the hallway. His polished shoes clicked against the smooth surface, echoing in the empty space.

"How much farther?" he called out irritably.

The guard gestured vaguely with one of its faceted appendages toward the end of the corridor. The hallway suddenly opened into a larger space, and the Crystalline stopped before a reinforced transparent barrier. "I still fail to comprehend the urgency," it chimed in its resonant, musical voice. "We have treated the prisoner with all appropriate protocols."

Miguel peered through the barrier into the holding cell. A figure huddled in the corner gradually came into focus—a thin, wiry man with sharp features and calculating eyes. "Isaac?" Miguel called sharply.

There was a startled gasp from within, and Isaac Hunt suddenly appeared at the barrier, his face breaking into a cunning smile beneath his unkempt hair. "Miguel! I knew they'd send you! I could count on it!" He performed an exaggerated bow. "Not much hospitality to offer, but it's the best I can manage under the circumstances."

Miguel frowned and turned to the guard. "Privacy, please. Interplanetary Protocol Article Seven. And leave the lighting."

The guard chimed its displeasure but departed. "About time you showed up!" Isaac cried. "Lucky they sent you, friend. I've been in here for weeks—"

"Look, Hunt, we're not friends," Miguel snapped. "And you've been here for exactly nineteen days, six hours, and approximately twenty minutes. You're getting as loose with facts as your Crystalline hosts." He studied Isaac's haggard appearance through the barrier. The man's eyes were bloodshot, his clothes disheveled. Miguel's expression softened slightly. "So Isaac Hunt's in trouble again. You look terrible."

Isaac snorted. "These silicon-based bureaucrats don't understand the concept of proper treatment. Synthetic nutrients and recycled water, nothing more. I thought you'd never arrive! I filed an appeal with the Earth Consulate the day I was detained. What took so long? All they had to do was process the extradition, sign the papers, and arrange transport off Lakeside Territory. Why the delay? I've been rotting here—" He stopped mid-sentence, his eyes widening. "You brought the papers, right? We can leave now?"

Miguel stared at the con artist with a mixture of pity and contempt. "You're a complete fool," he said finally. "Do you know that?"

Isaac's eyes narrowed. "What do you mean, fool? So I spend a few weeks in this freezer. The deal was worth it! I've pulled bigger schemes before—remember that fusion reactor scam back on Earth? Had accounts in three different banks there, and they never touched a credit of it. This time I was smarter. Kept it all in one place, right here where I could access it the moment I walked free." He grinned. "Five million credits! That's enough to retire on!"

Miguel nodded grimly. "If you live long enough to collect them, that is."

"What do you mean, if? The money's safe. Consulate protection—they can't touch accounts held under Earth jurisdiction."

"I'm not talking about the money. I'm talking about you."

Isaac's face fell. "What do you mean?"

Miguel moved closer to the barrier, his voice dropping to an intense whisper. "I mean that right now you are essentially a dead man. You may not realize it, but you are. You waltz onto a newly colonized territory with your bag of tricks, arrive here with questionable credentials and no proper authorization, with no understanding of the Crystalline culture beyond a few paragraphs of misinformation in the Colonial Guide. And even then, you're not satisfied with selling something legitimate, something the natives might actually need. No, nothing so straightforward for you. You have to run your usual high-pressure scheme. And this time, Hunt, you're paying the price."

"You mean I'm not being extradited?"

Miguel smiled coldly. "Exactly that. You've committed a crime here—a serious crime. The Crystallines are furious about it. And the Earth Consulate isn't willing to sacrifice all future trade possibilities just to bail you out. You're going to stand trial—and these beings want your head. Personally, I think they're going to get it."

Isaac stood shakily. "You can't trust anything they say. They operate on completely different principles than we do. You should see the deals they tried to make with me! I've never encountered such a complex negotiation system." He glanced up at Miguel. "They'll probably impose a fine and release me. I can cover any fine—I made sure to keep plenty accessible in the local consulate branch."

"A fine measured in your lifespan." Miguel's smile was unpleasant. "You've committed what they consider the gravest possible offense, and they're determined to see justice done. I'm afraid your con-artist days are over."

Isaac fumbled for a cigarette, lighting it with trembling hands. "It's bad, then."

"It's very bad."

Some hint of Isaac's usual sly grin returned. "Well, at least they sent you. Nothing like a good lawyer to handle a trial."

"Lawyer? Not me! Absolutely not!" Miguel laughed harshly. "I'm your advisor, nothing more. I'm here to prevent you from making things worse for the Trading Commission. That's all. I wouldn't get involved in a legal proceeding with these beings for anything!" He shook his head. "You're your own lawyer, Mr. Master-Salesman. It's your show. And you'd better start thinking clearly, or you're going to lose in ways you can't imagine!"

Miguel watched Isaac's pale face and shook his head. In a way, it was tragic to see such a transformation in the smooth-talking, confident little man who had talked his way out of more jams than Miguel could count. Trade expansion attracted scammers; it was inevitable that wherever rich and unexploited territories were opened, they would fall prey to fast-talking operators. They spread out from Earth with the first wave of colonization—the slick con artists who could work new territories unfettered by the legal restrictions that governed established colonies. The first ones in were the richest ones out, and through some peculiar quirk of human psychology, they knew they could count on Earth protection, however dishonest their methods.

Isaac had been one of the worst—or best, depending on perspective. Miguel had reviewed his file during the journey: seventeen confirmed schemes across six colonies, with suspected accounts scattered from Luna to the outer stations. His Earth accounts alone held proceeds from a dozen cons, though enforcement had never managed to freeze them. This Lakeside scheme was supposed to be his masterpiece, his retirement fund.

But occasionally a situation arose where the civilization and social practices of the alien inhabitants made interference unwise. Lakeside Territory had been recognized immediately by the Trading Commission as a commercial prize of tremendous value, but early reports had warned of the danger of wildcat trading on the crystalline world with its silicon-based, logic-driven inhabitants—warned specifically against the confidence tactics so frequently employed—but there was always someone, Miguel reflected bitterly, who didn't get the message.

Isaac puffed nervously on his cigarette, his narrow face troubled. "But I didn't do anything wrong!" he exploded. "So I ran a classic con. So what? Why are they so upset? So I made a few thousand credits, pulled some fast business." He shrugged eloquently. "Everyone does it. They do it to each other constantly. You should see how these beings operate with each other. My little scheme was nothing by comparison."

Miguel pulled out a pipe and began filling it methodically. "And precisely what sort of con game was it?" he asked quietly.

Isaac shrugged again. "The simplest, oldest scam in the book. Remember the old Earth story about selling the Brooklyn Bridge? Same concept. Only these beings didn't want bridges. They wanted energy—renewable energy sources for their expanding civilization. So I gave them what they wanted. I sold them energy rights."

Miguel nodded knowingly. "You certainly did. Exclusive rights to a hundred square kilometers of solar collection territory at a time. Only you sold the same hundred square kilometers to a dozen different Crystallines." Suddenly he threw back his head and laughed bitterly. "Of all the things you shouldn't have done—"

"But what's a patch of territory? The money flowed in beautifully. I had them deposit directly to the consulate account here in Nordavia—no cross-system transfers to trace, no delays, no complications."

Miguel shook his head hopelessly. "If you hadn't been so greedy, you'd have learned what territory means to these beings before you started peddling it. You'd have discovered other things about them, too. You'd have learned that despite all their logical processing and systematic behavior, they're not naive. You'd have found out that they're energy-dependent, and that three out of five newly formed Crystallines fail to secure sufficient energy sources to reach maturity. You'd have realized that they must compete for survival from the moment they crystallize. Anything goes, as long as it benefits them as individuals."

Miguel grinned at Isaac's horrified expression. "Never learned that, did you? And you've never learned other things, either. You probably never discovered that there are too many Crystallines here for the energy their territory can provide, and their energy requirements are so specific that they can't survive on anything that doesn't originate here. Consequently, territory is the fundamental factor in their economy, not currency; nothing but territory. To secure territory, it's every being for itself, and the loser dies, and their entire legal and economic system revolves around that principle. They've developed the most intricate and complex system of negotiation and exchange imaginable, aimed at individual survival, with territory as the value behind every transaction. That explains their approach to truth—of course they manipulate information, with an economy like that. They've completely redefined the concept of factual accuracy. Pathological? You bet they're pathological! Only a fool would present unvarnished truth when survival depends on being a more skillful negotiator than the next being! Information manipulation is their time-honored tradition, with their entire legal system built around it."

Isaac snorted. "But how could they possibly have a legal system? I mean, if they don't value straightforward truth?"

Miguel shrugged. "As we understand legal systems, I suppose they don't have one. They have only the vaguest notion what absolute truth represents, and they've dismissed the concept as impractical and useless." He chuckled maliciously. "So you went out and identified a section of solar collection territory, and sold exclusive rights to a dozen separate, self-centered, energy-starved Crystallines! Territorial encroachment is legal grounds for termination on this world, and twelve of them arrived at the same territory simultaneously, all armed with exclusive deeds." Miguel sighed. "You've got twelve furious Crystallines demanding justice. You've got an entire world demanding justice. And meanwhile, Earth's most valuable source of climate technology materials in decades is threatening to cut off supply unless they see you punished appropriately."

Isaac was visibly shaken. "Look," he said weakly, "so I made a mistake. What am I going to do? Are you going to stand by and let them destroy me? How could I defend myself in a legal system like this?"

Miguel smiled coolly. "You're going to get that devious little brain of yours working, I think," he said softly. "By Interplanetary Protocol, they have to give you a trial in Earth legal format—judge, jury, court procedure, all the standard elements. They think it's absurd—after all, what could a judicial oath mean to them?—but they agreed. The only problem is, they're determined to convict you, whatever it takes. So you'd better get those stunted wits of yours functioning—and if you try to implicate me, even slightly, I'll be gone so fast you won't know what happened."

With that, Miguel turned and walked toward the exit, leaving Isaac alone in the cold, sterile cell.

It certainly looked like a courtroom, at any rate. At the front of the large, temperature-controlled chamber was a bench with a seat behind it, and a small chair to the right. To the left was a platform with twelve seats—larger seats, with a railing along the front. The rest of the room was filled nearly to capacity with seats facing the bench. Isaac followed the Crystalline guard into the room, nodding approvingly. "Not a bad setup," he muttered. "They must have understood the concept quickly."

Miguel wiped the cold sweat from his forehead and shot Isaac a stern glance. "At least you've got a courtroom, a judge, and a jury. Beyond that—" He shrugged eloquently. "I can't make any promises."

At the back of the room, a door opened with a sharp hiss. Resonant, chiming voices filled the air as half a dozen Crystallines attempted to enter simultaneously. Isaac activated his translation device and watched the commotion in the anteroom with growing alarm. Finally, the question of precedence was resolved, and a group of Crystallines filed in, ordered by refraction index, moving across the room in flowing dark robes, their faceted faces gleaming with self-importance. They settled into the jury box, their crystalline bodies clicking against each other as they competed for front-row positions. The judge took his place with obvious satisfaction behind the heavy synthetic bench. Finally, the prosecuting attorney appeared, flanked by two assistants who took their positions beside him. The prosecutor fixed Isaac with a cold, multifaceted stare, then turned and performed what might have been a wink at the judge.

In moments, the room filled with the towering, geometric beings, their bodies refracting the harsh light as they jostled for seats, their chiming voices creating a cacophony of sound. Two minor altercations broke out in the rear but were quickly subdued by the security detail. Finally, the judge focused all his optical sensors on Isaac and struck the bench with a crystalline gavel until the activity subsided. The jurors shifted in their seats, exchanging what might have been knowing glances, then turned their attention forward.

"We are convening the case of the people of Lakeside Territory," the judge's voice resonated through the chamber, "against one Isaac Hunt—" he paused for a long, dramatic moment—"Earthman." The courtroom immediately erupted in angry chiming until the judge struck the bench several more times. "This—organism—is hereby accused of the following offenses," the judge announced. "Conspiracy to destabilize the government of Lakeside Territory. Deliberate termination of twenty-three law-abiding citizens of the settlement of Sunnydale, Ulvaria, during the third energy cycle following his arrival. Desecration of the Sacred Resonance Chamber of our revered Energy Matrix. Conspiracy with hostile elements to cause the unprecedented energy shortage in the Northern Sector. Deliberate exposure of his carbon-based physiology in a public space—" The judge struck the bench for order—"Espionage in coordination with the rival colony of Lakeside, Zelvaria, in preparation for territorial invasion."

Isaac's jaw dropped, the color draining from his face. He turned, wide-eyed, to Miguel, then back to the judge.

"The Jury Coordinator," said the judge efficiently, "will announce the verdict."

The Crystalline in the front of the jury box rose smoothly. "Defendant found guilty on all charges," it chimed.

"Defendant is guilty! The court will pronounce sentence—"

"Wait just a minute!" Isaac was on his feet, wild-eyed. "What kind of predetermined—"

The judge looked disappointedly at Miguel. "Not yet?" it asked, unhappily.

"No." Miguel's hands twitched nervously. "Not yet, Your Honor. Later, Your Honor. The trial comes first."

The judge appeared deflated. "But you indicated I should call for the verdict."

"Later. You must conduct the trial before you can have the verdict."

The Crystalline shrugged indifferently. "Now—later—" it chimed.

"Have the prosecutor call the first witness," said Miguel.

Isaac leaned over, his face ashen. "These charges," he whispered. "They're insane!"

"Of course they are," Miguel whispered back.

"But what am I going to—"

"Stay calm. Let them proceed."

"But those fabrications. They're all manipulating information, the entire system—" He broke off as the prosecutor resonated a name.

The Crystalline who took the stand was wearing a bright purple identification band that gleamed under the lights. It directed several optical sensors toward the prosecutor with what might have been anticipation. Then it began. "This Earthman criminal—"

"The oath," the judge interjected. "We must administer the oath."

The prosecutor nodded, and four Crystallines moved forward, carrying inscribed transparent tablets to the front of the court. One by one, the tablets were reverently stacked at the witness's base. The witness placed one faceted appendage on the stack, and the prosecutor said, "Do you swear to present information, complete information, and nothing but information, so help you—" he paused to consult the document in his appendage, finishing uncertainly, "—Energy Matrix?"

The witness removed the appendage from the tablets long enough to adjust its position, then replaced it and replied, "Of course," in an offended tone.

"Then present to this court what you have observed of the activities of this reprehensible being."

The witness settled back, focusing multiple sensors on Isaac's face, others on the prosecutor, and dimming a third set as if in contemplation. "I believe it occurred during the fourth cycle of the seventh rotation of Lakeside, Zelvaria (may the Energy Matrix deplete it)—or was it the seventh cycle of the fourth rotation?—" it directed a sensor apologetically at the judge—"when I was returning through the settlement toward my blessed territory, conducting my own affairs, Your Honor, after weeks of negotiating for the energy rights I was securing. Suddenly from the shadow of a structure, this creature—" it gestured an appendage at Isaac—"blocked my path with a threatening communication. He possessed a device I'd never encountered, and before I could process a response, he forced me against the wall. I could determine by the erratic patterns in his behavior that there was no logic, no systematic processing in his cognition, that I was—"

"Objection!" Isaac squealed, jumping to his feet. "This witness can't even remember what cycle he's talking about!"

The judge appeared startled. Then he searched frantically through his bundle of documents. "Overruled," he said abruptly. "Continue, please."

The witness directed all sensors at Isaac. "As I was stating before this disruptive interruption," it chimed, "I could determine that I was facing the most dangerous of criminal types, even for Earthmen. Note the asymmetry of his form, the irregularity of his features. I was paralyzed with concern. And then, helpless as I was, this two-legged abomination began to threaten harm to my blessed territory, dark threats of contaminating my energy sources unless I would reveal the location of our revered Energy Matrix—"

"I never encountered him before in my life," Isaac moaned to Miguel. "Listen to this! Why would I care where their Energy Matrix—"

Miguel gave him a hard look. "The Energy Matrix regulates everything here. It controls energy distribution. If it fails, someone's violated protocols. It's very straightforward."

"But how can I counter testimony like that?"

"I doubt you can counter it."

"But they can't verify any of it—" He looked at the jury, who were listening with rapt attention to the second witness. This one was testifying regarding the systematic destruction of twenty-three (or was it twenty-eight? Oh, yes, twenty-eight) Crystallines in the outlying settlement of Sunnydale. The massacre, it seemed, had been accomplished by a thermal weapon that caused catastrophic structural failure. A third witness took the stand, continuing the testimony as the room grew warmer and more oppressive. Isaac grew paler, his eyes becoming glassy as the accusations mounted. "But it's not true," he whispered to Miguel.

"Of course it isn't! Can't you understand? These beings have no regard for absolute truth. It's inefficient to them, foolish, a sign of poor processing. The only thing they respect is a negotiator more skillful and convincing than they are."

Isaac jerked around abruptly as he heard his name resonated. "Does the defendant have anything to present before the jury delivers the verdict?"

"Do I have—" Isaac was across the room in a flash, his pale cheeks suddenly flushed. He sat down carefully on the witness chair, facing the judge, his eyes bright with fear and excitement. "Your—Your Honor, I—I have information to present that will significantly impact this case. You must process it with the greatest attention." He glanced quickly at Miguel, then back to the judge. "Your Honor," he said in a hushed voice. "You are in the gravest danger. All of you. Your existence—your very territory is at stake."

The judge's optical sensors flickered, and he shuffled through his documents hurriedly as a murmur arose in the court. "Our territory?"

"Your existence, your territory, everything you value," Isaac said quickly, his words tumbling out. "You must attempt to understand me—" he glanced apprehensively over his shoulder—"now, because I may not survive long enough to repeat what I am about to reveal—"

The murmur quieted, all attention focused on his words through the translation devices. "These charges," he continued, "all of them—they're completely accurate. At least, they appear to be completely accurate. But in every instance, I was operating with full commitment, risking my existence, for the welfare of your magnificent territory."

There was a loud hiss of static from the back of the court. Isaac frowned and rubbed his hands together. "It was my misfortune," he said, "to arrive at the wrong colony when I first came to Lakeside from my homeland on Earth. I—I landed on Lakeside, Zelvaria, a serious error, but as it turned out, a very fortunate mistake. Because in attempting to establish trade in that hostile place, I made certain connections." His voice trembled and dropped lower. "I learned the terrible thing that is about to happen to this territory, at the hands of those rivals. The conspiracy is theirs, not mine. They have corrupted your Energy Matrix, manipulated it and deceived it, subverted its all-powerful regulation to their own malicious interests, preparing for the day when they could convince it to cast your territory into the catastrophic darkness of a ten-cycle energy blackout—"

Someone in the middle of the court burst into resonant laughter. One by one, the Crystallines nudged each other and chimed their amusement until the rising tide of noise drowned out Isaac's words. "The defendant is obviously manipulating information," the prosecutor resonated over the pandemonium. "Any properly functioning being knows that the Energy Matrix cannot be corrupted. How could it be an Energy Matrix if it could?"

Isaac grew paler. "But—perhaps they were very sophisticated—"

"And how could they manipulate it, when it processes, beyond any doubt, that it is the most perfectly calibrated system in all the Universe? And you dare to insult it, impugn its integrity."

The hisses grew louder, more hostile. Cries of "Terminate him!" and "Dissolve his structure!" rose from the courtroom. The judge struck for silence, his sensors angry.

"Unless the defendant wishes to consume more of our valuable processing time with these absurd manipulations, the jury—"

"Wait! Your Honor, I request a brief recess before I present my final statement."

"Recess?"

"A few moments to organize my thoughts, to structure my defense."

The judge settled back with a disgusted chime. "Must I?" he asked Miguel.

Miguel nodded. The judge shrugged, gesturing toward the anteroom. "You may use that chamber," he said.

Somehow, Isaac managed to stumble from the witness stand, amid riotous hisses and chimes, and staggered into the anteroom.

Isaac inhaled deeply from his cigarette and looked up at Miguel with haunted eyes. "It—it doesn't look promising," he muttered.

Miguel's eyes were troubled, too. For some reason, he felt a surge of sympathy and respect for the haggard con artist. "It's worse than I anticipated," he admitted grimly. "That was a good attempt, but you simply don't understand enough about them and their Energy Matrix." He sat down wearily. "I don't see what you can do. They want justice, and they're determined to get it. They simply won't believe you, no matter how skillfully you manipulate information."

Isaac sat in silence for a moment. "This information manipulation business," he said finally, "exactly how does it function?"

"The most skillful, most convincing negotiator wins. It's that simple. It doesn't matter how elaborate a construction you present. Unless, of course, they've determined that you simply aren't as skillful a negotiator as they are. And it appears that's exactly what they've concluded. It wouldn't matter what you present—unless, somehow, you could make them believe it."

Isaac frowned. "And how do they regard the—the most skillful negotiator? I mean, how do they respond to him?"

Miguel shifted uncomfortably. "It's difficult to say. It's been my experience that they respect him highly—perhaps even fear him somewhat. After all, the most convincing negotiator always wins in any transaction, so he secures more territory, more energy, more power. Yes, I think the most skillful negotiator could operate without any interference."

Isaac was on his feet, his eyes suddenly bright with excitement. "Wait a moment," he said tensely. "To present them with information that they'd have to accept—information they simply couldn't help but accept—" He turned on Miguel, his hands trembling. "Do they process the way we do? I mean, with logic, cause and effect, examining evidence and drawing conclusions? Given certain evidence, would they have to draw the same conclusions that we would draw?"

Miguel blinked. "Well—yes. Absolutely, they're perfectly logical."

Isaac's eyes flashed, and a huge grin broke across his haggard face. His thin body trembled. He started pacing excitedly, staring into space. "If I could only remember—" he muttered. "Someone—somewhere—something I studied."

"Whatever are you talking about?"

"It was a philosopher, I think—"

Miguel stared at him. "Oh, come now. Have you lost your mind completely? You have a serious problem here."

"No, no, I've solved the problem!" Isaac's cheeks flushed. "Let's return—I think I have the answer!"

The courtroom quieted the moment they opened the door, and the judge struck the gavel for silence. As soon as Isaac had taken his seat on the witness stand, the judge turned to the Jury Coordinator. "Now, then," he said with satisfied finality. "The jury—"

"Hold on! Just one moment more."

The judge stared down at Isaac as if he were a malfunctioning component. "Oh, yes. You had additional information to present. Well, proceed and present it."

Isaac looked sharply around the hushed room. "You want to convict me," he said softly, "in the most complete way possible. Isn't that correct?"

Sensors swung toward him. The judge's facets gleamed with anticipation. "That's correct."

"But you can't properly convict me until you've carefully processed any information I present in my own defense. Isn't that correct?"

The judge appeared uncomfortable. "If you have information to present, proceed and present it."

"I have just one statement to make. Brief and direct. But you'd better process it, and analyze it carefully before you decide that you really want to convict me." He paused and directed his gaze at the judge. "You don't value those who present unprocessed truth, it seems. Well, enter this statement in your record, then." His voice was loud and clear in the still room. "All Earthmen are absolutely incapable of presenting accurate information."

Puzzled expressions appeared on the jury's faceted faces. One or two exchanged startled glances, and the room was silent as death. The judge stared at him, then at Miguel, then back. "But you"—he stammered. "You're"—He stopped mid-sentence, his sensors flickering wildly.

One of the jurors let out a small chime and went completely dark. It took, all in all, about ten seconds for the statement to register.

And then chaos erupted in the courtroom.

"Really," said Isaac Hunt smugly, "it was so obvious I'm amazed it didn't occur to me immediately." He settled himself comfortably in the control cabin of the transport vessel and grinned at the outline of Lakeside, Nordavia growing larger in the viewscreen.

Miguel Ortiz stared stonily at the controls, his lips compressed angrily. "You might at least have informed me of your plan."

"And risk being monitored? Don't be ridiculous. It had to be a complete surprise. I had to establish myself as an information manipulator—the supreme manipulator of them all, but I had to present the sort of information that they simply could not process. Something that would throw them into such utter logical contradiction that they wouldn't dare convict me." He grinned impishly at Miguel. "The paradox of Epimenides the Cretan. It really stopped them cold. They knew I was an Earthman, which meant that my statement that Earthmen couldn't present accurate information was inaccurate, which meant that maybe I could present accurate information, in which case—oh, it was perfect."

"It sure was." Miguel's voice was a snarl.

"Well, it established me as a negotiator in a class they couldn't match, didn't it?"

Miguel's face was purple with anger. "Oh, indeed it did! And it classified all Earthmen in exactly the same category, too."

"So what's honor among thieves? I got off, didn't I? And now we're heading to Nordavia so I can finally collect my money. Should have transferred it back to my accounts on Earth—would have been safer—but I got greedy, wanted to avoid the cross-system fees."

Miguel turned on him fiercely. "Oh, you got off just fine. You terrified them completely. And in an eon of information manipulation, they've never encountered a logical paradox like that. You've also completely destroyed any hope of ever establishing a trading alliance with Lakeside Territory, and that includes climate technology materials, too. Intelligent beings don't engage with loaded systems. You frightened them so thoroughly they want nothing to do with us."

Isaac's grin broadened, and he leaned back luxuriously. "Ah, well. After all, the Trading Alliance was your concern, wasn't it? What a shame!" He clicked his tongue sadly. "Me, I've got a fortune in credits sitting at the consulate in Nordavia waiting for me—enough to keep me comfortable for quite a while, I must say. I think I'll just take a nice, long vacation."

Miguel turned to him, and a glint of malicious satisfaction appeared in his eyes. "Yes, I think you will. I'm quite certain of it, in fact. Won't cost you a credit, either."

"What?"

Miguel grinned unpleasantly. He brushed an imaginary speck from his lapel and looked up at Isaac slyly. "That—uh—jury trial. The Crystallines weren't particularly happy to accommodate. They wanted to terminate you immediately. Thought a trial was completely inefficient—until they recovered their investment, of course. Not excessive—just five million credits."

Isaac went white. "But that money was in protected custody! Earth Consulate jurisdiction—they couldn't touch it!"

"Is that so? My goodness. You don't suppose they could have misplaced those custody documents, do you? Funny thing about the consulate branch here in Nordavia—they've been quite cooperative with local authorities lately. Trade relations, you understand." Miguel grinned at the little con artist. "And incidentally, you're under arrest, you know."

A choking sound came from Isaac's throat. "Arrest!"

"Oh, yes. Didn't I mention it? Conspiring to undermine the authority of the Earth Trading Commission. Serious charge, you know. Yes, I think we'll take a nice long journey together, straight back to Earth. And there I think you'll face a jury trial."

Isaac spluttered. "There's no evidence—you've got nothing on me! What kind of setup are you trying to pull?"

"A beautiful setup. Airtight. A case from the ground up, and you're right in the center of it. And this time—" Miguel tapped a cigarette on his thumb with satisfied finality—"this time I don't think you'll get off."
problem_data.question: Where was the five million credits Isaac Hunt mentioned held?
problem_data.correct_answer: At the Earth Consulate at Lakeside, Nordavia
problem_data.incorrect_answer: In a secret account on Earth
answers: In a secret account on Earth
At the Earth Consulate at Lakeside, Nordavia
